---
title: netstead
audience: users
kind: concept
summary: Python toolkit for the General Modeling Network Specification — build, load, validate, scope, edit and explore GMNS networks at regional scale, with CLI / notebook / browser Workbench / HTTP / MCP surfaces. Built on corral.
---

# netstead

A Python toolkit for the [General Modeling Network Specification (GMNS)](https://github.com/zephyr-data-specs/GMNS) — the Zephyr Foundation's open standard for routable transportation networks. Built on top of [corral](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/).

![Sixty-second walkthrough: open, select, validate, fix, replay](assets/screenshots/workbench-walkthrough.gif){ .screenshot }
*The browser Workbench in a minute: open a network, select by name, validate, fix a finding, replay it all as Python. Start with [Quickstart: the Workbench](quickstart-workbench.md).*

[![Open In Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/netstead/docs/notebooks/quickstart.ipynb) — five-cell quickstart in the browser. The first cell installs from GitHub; the rest load a real GMNS network from a URL, validate it, and view findings on an interactive map. Nothing to set up locally.

## What problems netstead solves

**Reading any GMNS network without writing import code.** Local CSV directory, S3 parquet partition, single-file DuckDB, zipped CSV bundle — same `Network.from_source(...)` call, same lazy-evaluation behavior:

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
from netstead import Network

net = Network.from_source("./my-network/")              # CSV directory
net = Network.from_source("s3://bucket/network.parquet/")  # cloud parquet
net = Network.from_source("./network.duckdb")              # single duckdb
```

**Validation in one report.** `net.validate()` covers structural (required tables), schema (per-field constraints), foreign-key (cross-table integrity), and sync-state (have FKs gone stale since the last edit?). Severity-graded, rendered as rich console / JSON / interactive HTML.

**Data quality beyond the spec.** Nine rules out of the box — high-speed-on-residential, disconnected components, lane-count mismatch, near-duplicate nodes, sharp-angle bends, implausible v/c ratios, missing critical fields, overlapping links, and repeated rows that should be unique (e.g. two `link_tod` rows for one link and time window). Plug in your own with a class + entry point.

**Network-aware scope** at regional scale. BFS-induced subgraph from seed nodes, Dijkstra-bounded network buffer, spatial-buffer from any link or point, connected-component, zone filter. Chainable, with FK pushdown to every related table (TOD overrides, lane detail, signal control).

**Editing with atomic rollback.** `with Session(net) as s: simplify_geometry(net, s); merge_close_nodes(net, s)` — commit on clean exit, roll back on exception. Pass `log_path=` to persist the edit log as a sidecar file you can replay later.

**Building networks from open data.** `netstead build --source osm` (or `--source overture`) turns a place name, bbox, or point + buffer into a validated GMNS node + link network — no import code, no manual tag mapping.

**Exploring in a browser Workbench.** `netstead app` opens a local app with a linked map and tables, validation with proposed fixes, selection verification, and a natural-language assistant that drafts actions for you to approve.

**Natural-language selection.** `netstead select` resolves a plain-English description ("residential links north of the river") to GMNS link / node ids, through Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, or a local Ollama model (the `[nl]` extra).

**Surfaces for every workflow.** CLI for shells and scripts, notebook `_repr_html_` for Jupyter, the browser Workbench for interactive exploration, FastAPI HTTP server for self-hosting, MCP server for Claude Desktop / Claude Code; every data command supports `--json`.

## Use cases — when to install netstead

<div class="grid cards" markdown>

-   :material-map:{ .lg .middle } &nbsp;**MPO / DOT planning**

    ---

    Loading regional networks from OSM-derived sources, validating against the spec, applying data-quality checks before they feed a model.

-   :material-truck-fast-outline:{ .lg .middle } &nbsp;**Travel-demand modeling**

    ---

    Scoping a regional GMNS network down to a project area or analysis subnet, exporting to your modeling tool's format with zero conversion code.

-   :material-pencil-ruler:{ .lg .middle } &nbsp;**Network editing**

    ---

    Cleaning up an OSM-extract before it goes into a model — simplify geometry, merge near-duplicate nodes, remove orphans, recompute lengths.

-   :material-robot-outline:{ .lg .middle } &nbsp;**AI-assisted analysis**

    ---

    Letting Claude (or any MCP-compatible agent) drive validation, quality checks, and scope queries through a tool-call loop.

-   :material-server-network:{ .lg .middle } &nbsp;**Self-hosted network API**

    ---

    Exposing a curated set of GMNS networks behind a FastAPI HTTP server with bearer-token auth for consumers in your organization.

-   :material-school-outline:{ .lg .middle } &nbsp;**GTFS-GMNS interop research**

    ---

    Researching the bridge between transit schedules and routable street networks; netstead gives you the GMNS side as a stable substrate.

</div>

## Why install netstead

**GMNS spec built in.** Vendored 0.95 / 0.96 / 0.97 side-by-side. Default 0.97; per-call override `Network.from_source(path, spec_version="0.96")`. Networks load against the version they were written against — no silent upgrades.

**Regional scale on a laptop.** Lazy ibis + DuckDB by default. A 200k-node network reads in seconds and validates in tens of seconds. Spatial and graph indexes built on demand, cached to sidecar parquet, content-hash keyed for auto-invalidation.

**Four usage modes target the same data.** CLI, notebook, programmatic, browser Workbench — choose by ergonomics, not capability.

**AI-first by design.** Every data command supports `--json` for tool-call loops. `llms.txt` + `llms-full.txt` + `ai/api-index.json` regenerate on every docs build. Optional MCP server (`netstead mcp serve`) for Claude Desktop / Claude Code. Six Claude Code Skills shipped in-repo.

**No vendor lock-in.** Pure Python under Apache 2.0. Formats, quality rules, scope ops all behind protocols you can implement yourself.

## Install

Requires Python 3.11+. `netstead` 1.0.0b2 is not on PyPI yet (the first release under the new names is pending), so one command installs both packages from GitHub, with every optional extra:

```bash
uv init --bare
uv add \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead[all] @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"
```

`uv init --bare` makes a new folder a uv project, which `uv add` needs; skip it when you add netstead to a project you already have.

The four install tools (uv, uv pip, pip, pipx), the full table of extras and what each pulls in, `netstead doctor`, and the first-run errors are all on one page: [Install and troubleshoot](install.md). zsh users: [quote the brackets](install.md#zsh-quote-the-brackets).

---
title: "Quickstart: Python"
audience: users
kind: howto
summary: Install, load the bundled Leavenworth fixture, run validation + quality + scope from Python in five minutes.
---

# Quickstart: Python

Prefer a browser? → [Quickstart: the Workbench](quickstart-workbench.md) does the same work with no code.

## When to use this

You're new to `netstead` and want to see what it does on a real GMNS network before reading anything else. Time budget: five minutes.

## Quick example

The fastest way to confirm `netstead` is wired up correctly is to install it, load the bundled Leavenworth, WA fixture, and print a one-line summary. `netstead` 1.0.0b2 is not on PyPI yet, so the beta installs from GitHub (both packages in one command; see [Install and troubleshoot](install.md)):

```bash
pip install \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead[clean,graph] @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"
```

Then in Python:

```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
print(f"{net.spec_version}: {net.links.count()} links, {net.nodes.count()} nodes")
```

Expected:

```text
0.97: 339 links, 121 nodes
```

You just loaded the bundled Leavenworth network through the default ibis + DuckDB engine. Nothing was materialized — `net.links` is a lazy expression; only the integer count came back from DuckDB to Python.

## Step-by-step

### 1. Install

The bare `netstead` install is enough for read-only validation. Add `[clean,graph]` to unlock the ops the rest of this guide uses: `[clean]` brings in `shapely` + `geopandas` + `pyproj` for the geometry edits; `[graph]` brings in `scipy` (+ `numpy` + `pandas`) for the scope graph, connected components, and the data-quality rule pack.

```bash
uv init --bare
uv add \
  "dbcorral @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/corral" \
  "netstead[clean,graph] @ git+https://github.com/e-lo/netstead.git@main#subdirectory=packages/netstead"
```

`uv init --bare` makes a new folder a uv project, which `uv add` needs; skip it when you add netstead to a project you already have.

This is the GitHub form the beta uses until the PyPI release is out; it then becomes `uv add 'netstead[clean,graph]'`, with `corral` coming along as a transitive dependency. For the other install tools (uv pip, pip, pipx), the full list of extras and what each pulls in, `netstead doctor`, and the zsh bracket-quoting rule, see [Install and troubleshoot](install.md).

### 2. Load the bundled fixture

The fixture is a small real network (Leavenworth, WA — an OSM-derived street grid roughly 2 km across) bundled inside the `netstead` wheel, so the example below runs without any download. `Network.from_source` accepts the same surface as `corral.Package.from_source`: local paths, URLs (`s3://`, `https://`, `duckdb://`), or directories of CSV / Parquet / DuckDB / zip-CSV.

```python
from netstead import Network
from netstead.fixtures import leavenworth

net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir())
```

The result is a lazy `Network` object — its tables haven't been read yet. Print a quick summary to confirm it loaded:

```python
print(f"{net.spec_version}: {net.links.count()} links, {net.nodes.count()} nodes")
```

Expected:

```text
0.97: 339 links, 121 nodes
```

In a Jupyter notebook, evaluating `net` on its own renders an HTML summary card with the spec version, per-table row counts, and a preview of the first rows.

![Network summary card](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-network-card.png){ .screenshot }
*Network summary card (net._repr_html_() in a notebook) — spec version, table inventory with row counts, first-rows preview*

### 3. Validate against the spec

Validation runs four passes in a single call: **structural** (required tables and files), **schema** (per-field types and constraints), **foreign-key** (cross-table integrity), and **sync-state** (have any FKs gone stale since a previous edit?). The Leavenworth fixture has no ERRORs, but it is not spotless: expect 16 INFO findings (`structural.missing_optional_resource`, one per optional GMNS table the fixture doesn't ship) and 1 WARNING (`fk.unverifiable`: `node.zone_id` can't be checked because there is no `zone` table). That WARNING is why `report.is_clean` is `False` — `is_clean` means no ERRORs *and* no WARNINGs.

```python
report = net.validate()
print(f"issues: {len(report.issues)} ({report.spec_version})")
```

In a notebook, `report` on its own renders an HTML card grouped by severity.

![Validation report card](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-validation-report.png){ .screenshot }
*Validation report card (report._repr_html_() in a notebook) — 0 ERRORs, 0 WARNINGs, 16 INFO structural.missing_optional_resource*

### 4. Run data-quality checks

The data-quality rule pack covers things the spec is silent on but every real network gets wrong sooner or later. Its nine rules cover high-speed-residential, lane-count mismatch, sharp-angle bends, near-duplicate nodes, disconnected components, implausible v/c ratios, missing critical fields, overlapping links and non-unique combinations (see [Customize the quality pack](cookbook/customize-quality.md)). Findings come back as WARNING or INFO by default and carry `category=DATA_QUALITY`. The rule pack needs the `[graph]` extra. On Leavenworth, `quality.high_speed_residential` fires on 271 residential links whose `free_speed` is 40 — above the default 35 mph threshold.

```python
from corral.quality import run_quality

qreport = run_quality(net)
for issue in qreport.issues[:5]:
    print(f"  {issue.severity.value:9} {issue.code:35} {issue.message[:60]}")
```

![Quality report card](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-quality-report.png){ .screenshot }
*Quality report card (qreport._repr_html_() in a notebook) — 271 WARNING quality.high_speed_residential findings on residential links with free_speed=40 at the default 35 mph threshold*

### 5. Scope to a subgraph

The scope module lets you carve a smaller network out of a larger one without writing FK-pushdown SQL by hand. `from_node` builds a network-distance-bounded subgraph around a seed node; every related table (`lane`, `link_tod`, `movement`, signal control) is pre-filtered so the result is still a self-consistent GMNS network.

<!-- doctest: skip -->
```python
from netstead.scope import from_node

scoped = from_node(net, 1, network_buffer="200m").apply()
print(f"scoped: {scoped.links.count()} links, {scoped.nodes.count()} nodes")
```

That's a 200-metre Dijkstra-bounded buffer around node 1. Expected:

```text
scoped: 8 links, 5 nodes
```

![Scoped subgraph](assets/screenshots/leavenworth-scoped-map.png){ .screenshot }
*Scoped subgraph (200 m network buffer around node 1, green) over the full Leavenworth network (grey context)*

### 6. Or run the same thing from the CLI

The CLI mirrors the Python API one-for-one. The same fixture lives at `packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv` in the repo, so you can point the CLI at it directly.

```bash
netstead info packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
netstead validate packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
netstead quality packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv
netstead scope from-node packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv 1 --network-buffer 200m
```

`quality` and `scope` need the `[graph]` extra; `info` and `validate` run on the bare install.

By default `netstead` prints colorized tables and panels for humans. Add `--json` and you get a single machine-readable JSON document on stdout instead — useful for scripting, CI checks, or feeding the output to an AI agent.

```bash
netstead validate --json packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/csv | jq '.issues | length'
```

## Common variations

Each accordion below is one alternative to the defaults used above. The first (most common) is expanded; the rest are collapsed — open the one that matches your situation.

???+ note "Pick a different GMNS spec version"
    The vendored versions are 0.95, 0.96, and 0.97; default is 0.97. Networks load against the version they were written against — no silent upgrades.

    ```python
    net = Network.from_source(leavenworth.csv_dir(), spec_version="0.96")
    ```

??? note "Get a pandas (or polars) frame"
    DuckDB (via ibis) is the only compute engine, and every table stays lazy until you ask. When downstream code wants a DataFrame, materialize just that table with `.to_pandas()` or `.to_polars()`.

    ```python
    links_df = net.links.to_pandas()
    ```

??? note "Read from S3 with credentials"
    Credentials resolve via a cascade: keyword arg → `CORRAL_CRED_<host>_TOKEN` env var → OS keyring → `.netrc`. No code changes if your environment is already set up.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

    ```python
    net = Network.from_source("s3://bucket/network/")
    ```

??? note "Write the scoped network out"
    The output format follows the destination: an extension-less path or `.parquet` writes a directory of GeoParquet files (one per table); `.csv` writes a CSV directory; `.duckdb` writes a single DuckDB file; `.zip` writes zipped CSV.
<!-- doctest: skip -->

    ```python
    scoped.write("./scoped.parquet")
    ```

??? note "Run the data-quality pack with custom thresholds"
    Per-rule config keys override defaults. The example below tightens the residential-speed threshold to 30 mph.

    ```python
    from corral.quality import RuleConfig, run_quality

    qreport = run_quality(
        net,
        config={
            "quality.high_speed_residential": RuleConfig(
                thresholds={"speed_limit_mph": 30.0}
            )
        },
    )
    ```

## Pitfalls

* **Auto-build of the graph index on large networks.** The first `from_node` or `connected_component` call on a network larger than 50k nodes builds the scipy `GMNSGraph` adjacency on the spot and logs an INFO notice. Pre-build with `net.build_indexes(graph=True)` if you want to control the timing, or set `NETSTEAD_AUTO_INDEX_THRESHOLD` to raise the auto-build bar.
* **Duplicate-near-nodes default threshold is tight** (`epsilon_units=1e-5`). Networks in WGS84 degrees barely trigger it; networks in projected meters need an explicit threshold via `RuleConfig`.
* **Editing requires a `Session`.** Don't mutate tables directly — open `with corral.editing.Session(net) as s:` and pass `s` into the `netstead.clean.*` ops. See [Edit a network with atomic rollback](cookbook/edit-with-rollback.md).

## See also

* [Cookbook](cookbook/index.md) — task-oriented recipes for the common workflows.
* [Python tour (notebook)](python-tour.md) — see every step above rendered as maps, cards, and diffs in a notebook.
* [Visual tour](visual-tour.md) — the same network in the browser Workbench, screen by screen.

<!-- source: what-is-gmns.md url: https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/netstead/what-is-gmns.md -->

---
title: What is GMNS?
audience: both
kind: concept
summary: Plain-English introduction to the General Modeling Network Specification — what it defines, who maintains it, how it relates to Frictionless, GTFS, and OpenStreetMap.
---

# What is GMNS?

## What it is

The **General Modeling Network Specification (GMNS)** is an open standard, maintained by the [Zephyr Foundation](https://zephyrtransport.org/), for representing routable transportation networks as a small set of related tables. The spec lives at [github.com/zephyr-data-specs/GMNS](https://github.com/zephyr-data-specs/GMNS) and is versioned (current vendored versions: 0.95, 0.96, 0.97).

A GMNS network is a directory of CSVs (or Parquet, or any tabular store) plus a `datapackage.json` manifest that describes the schema. The required core is just two tables:

* `link` — directed edges of the routable graph (one row per road segment between two intersections).
* `node` — vertices of the graph (intersections, dead-ends, zone centroids).

Layered on top of that core, the spec defines optional tables for the things real transportation models need:

* **Geometry detail** — `geometry` (WKT shapes per link), `segment` and `segment_lane` (sub-link partitioning for places where lane geometry changes).
* **Lane detail** — `lane` (one row per travel lane), `movement` (turning movements at a node).
* **Time-of-day overrides** — `link_tod`, `lane_tod`, `segment_tod`, `segment_lane_tod`, `movement_tod` — per-period overrides on capacity, allowed uses, lane assignments.
* **Signal control** — `signal_controller`, `signal_coordination`, `signal_detector`, `signal_phase_mvmt`, `signal_timing_phase`, `signal_timing_plan`.
* **Demand context** — `zone` (traffic analysis zones), `location` (curb-side points), `curb_seg` (curb space management).
* **Dimension tables** — `time_set_definitions` (period definitions), `use_definition` and `use_group` (vehicle / mode classes), `config` (network-wide configuration).

The full set across the 0.97 spec is **25 resource files**. See [Table of tables](reference/table-of-tables.md) for the catalog and [Schema reference](reference/spec.md) for field-level detail.

The spec ships as a [Frictionless Data Package](https://specs.frictionlessdata.io/data-package/) — `datapackage.json` declares each resource, its CSV schema, primary keys, and foreign-key relationships in a machine-readable form.

## Why we have it

Before GMNS, every traffic simulator, travel-demand model, and routing engine carried its own network format. A network exported from Cube didn't load in TransCAD; a Visum file didn't open in SUMO; a TomTom routing graph wasn't a TransModeler input. Modelers spent more time writing conversion scripts than running models, and every conversion silently dropped information.

GMNS exists so a network produced for one tool travels to another with **zero conversion code**. The interop story is the whole story:

1. Producers (state DOTs, MPOs, OSM derivative pipelines) publish in GMNS.
2. Consumers (modelers, routing services, analysis tools) read GMNS directly.
3. The spec is small enough that bespoke conversions are practical when a tool *doesn't* speak GMNS natively — but the goal is that they don't have to be written twice.

GMNS is **not** a modeling format with semantics baked in (capacity calculations, BPR functions, signal optimisation). It is the *substrate* on which those tools operate. The same GMNS network feeds a microsimulation, a static-equilibrium assignment, and an active-transportation accessibility analysis.

## Mental model

* **Tables, not files** — a GMNS network is a set of relations, not a binary blob. Any tabular store works (CSV, Parquet, DuckDB, zipped CSV).
* **Two required tables, the rest optional** — the minimum viable GMNS network is `link` + `node`. Every other table layers detail onto that spine.
* **Foreign keys are the API** — relationships between tables (`lane.link_id` → `link.link_id`, `link.from_node_id` → `node.node_id`) are declared in `datapackage.json` and machine-checkable.

The core relationships:

```mermaid
erDiagram
    node ||--o{ link : "from_node_id / to_node_id"
    link ||--o{ lane : "link_id"
    link ||--o{ link_tod : "link_id"
    link }o--|| geometry : "geometry_id (optional)"
    node ||--o{ movement : "node_id"
    link ||--o{ movement : "ib_link_id / ob_link_id"
```

A real network has more edges in this diagram (signal tables hang off `node`, segment tables sub-divide `link`, zone tables hang off `node`) but the four cardinal relations above carry most of the routing semantics.

## How it relates to ...

### The Frictionless Data Package format

GMNS is a Frictionless Data Package. The spec is not a custom serialization — it's a `datapackage.json` that declares 25 resources, each with a Table Schema (field types, constraints, primary key, foreign keys). Any Frictionless-compatible reader can parse a GMNS package's structure without knowing what GMNS is.

This is why the Netstead validator's structural and schema passes are inherited verbatim from `corral` (the generic toolkit underneath); only the foreign-key chains and the data-quality rules are GMNS-specific.

### GTFS

[GTFS](https://gtfs.org/) (General Transit Feed Specification) is a separate spec, scoped to **scheduled public transit** — routes, stops, trips, stop-times. GMNS is scoped to the **routable roadway / street network** — links, nodes, lanes, signals.

The two are complementary and frequently combined: GMNS for the street network the bus drives on, GTFS for the bus schedule. Bridging tools like [openmobilitydata.org](https://openmobilitydata.org) and the in-development GTFS-GMNS reconciliation patterns let a transit assignment use both.

GMNS deliberately does not duplicate GTFS. A `transit_route` table is *not* in GMNS — that's GTFS's job.

### OpenStreetMap

[OpenStreetMap (OSM)](https://www.openstreetmap.org/) is a global, crowdsourced geographic database. It is **not** a network spec — OSM tags are loose, regionally inconsistent, and not designed for routing-grade modeling out of the box.

GMNS is the standardized target for the conversion. Tools like [`osm2gmns`](https://github.com/jiawlu/OSM2GMNS) and `osmnx` (used to build the bundled Leavenworth fixture — see its [README](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/leavenworth/README.md)) consume OSM, infer link attributes (lanes, free-flow speed, facility type) from OSM tags, and emit GMNS. netstead's own Overture builder produced the bundled Market Street, San Francisco fixture (Overture Maps, an ODbL-licensed OpenStreetMap derivative; see its [README](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/netstead/netstead/fixtures/market_street/README.md)).

OSM → GMNS is lossy and opinionated (tag inference is heuristic; OSM doesn't carry signal timing or TOD restrictions). The point is that the *output* is a single standardized format that every downstream consumer understands, regardless of where the source data came from.

## See also

* [Quickstart](quickstart.md) — install and load the bundled fixture in five minutes.
* [Python tour (notebook)](python-tour.md) — see Leavenworth rendered as a map, validated, edited, and scoped from Python.
* [Visual tour](visual-tour.md) — the same network in the browser Workbench, screen by screen.
* [Table of tables](reference/table-of-tables.md) — catalog of every GMNS resource.
* [Schema reference](reference/spec.md) — field-level reference for the upstream GMNS spec (vendored 0.97 when offline).
* [Architecture](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/architecture/) — design rationale for the toolkit on top of GMNS.

---

<!-- screenshots: refresh after the beta-feedback PR merges -->

# Visual tour

This is the [Workbench quickstart](quickstart-workbench.md) told slowly: the same eight steps on the same
bundled network, but with the emphasis on what you are looking at, what netstead is doing underneath, and why
it matters for a real network. The notebook version of this tour, with maps and report cards rendered from
Python, is the [Python tour](python-tour.md).

## What you'll build

![Sixty-second walkthrough: open, select, validate, fix, replay](assets/screenshots/workbench-walkthrough.gif){ .screenshot }
*Open, select, validate, fix, replay: the tour in a minute. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

By the end you will be able to read the Workbench the way a modeler reads it: a GMNS network on a map, its
tables beside it, a selection with a status you can trust, a validation report whose severities mean something,
an edit log with versions, and a script that reproduces all of it.

## Prerequisites

Follow step 1 of the [Workbench quickstart](quickstart-workbench.md#1-install-and-open-the-network) to install
`netstead` with the `[server,graph,nl]` extras and open the Leavenworth fixture with `--provider stub`. This
page doesn't repeat the commands; if the install or the first run fails, see
[Install and troubleshoot](install.md).

## Steps

### 1. A GMNS network on a map

![The Workbench with the Leavenworth network open](assets/screenshots/workbench-01-open.png){ .screenshot }
*Leavenworth, WA: 339 links and 121 nodes, drawn from the `link`, `node` and `geometry` tables. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

What you see is a small, real street network: downtown Leavenworth, an OSM-derived grid about 2 km across,
with Highway 2 along the south and residential streets fanning north. The header says what it is made of:
**339 links · 121 nodes**. In GMNS a **node** is a point (an intersection, a dead end, a change of attributes)
and a **link** is a directed edge between two nodes with the attributes a model needs: `facility_type`,
`lanes`, `free_speed`, `capacity`, `directed`. Each link's shape comes from the `geometry` table, keyed by
`geometry_id`, which is why a link can bend without extra nodes.

Why it matters: everything else in the Workbench is a view of those tables. The map is not a separate GIS
layer that can drift from the data; it is drawn from the `link` rows you are about to edit, and it redraws
when they change. If the map opened zoomed out, **Zoom to full network** fits the view to the network's
bounding box: the first thing to try whenever the map looks empty.

### 2. The linked table

![Split view: a link picked on the map, its row focused in the table](assets/screenshots/workbench-02-split.png){ .screenshot }
*Split view. One record, three views: the link on the map, its row in the table, its attributes in Inspect. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

**Split** puts the `link` table next to the map. The rail on the left of the table lists every table in the
network with its row count: `link`, `node`, `geometry`, `lane`, `link_tod` and the rest. Click a link on the
map and three things agree on which record you mean: the map outlines it, the table scrolls to and outlines
its row, and the **Inspect** tab comes forward and lists its attributes. Click a row and the map flies to it.

What the linked table gives you is the half of a network that a map can't show. A speed, a lane count, a
time-of-day override or a foreign key are table facts; the map can color by one of them at a time (**Find →
View → Color links by**), but the table shows them all, sortable and pageable, with the key columns (`from_node_id`,
`geometry_id`) as links you can follow into the other tables. Rows a foreign key away from the focused record,
such as the link's two end nodes or its lanes, are tinted in every table and on the map. GMNS is a relational
spec, and the Workbench treats it as one.

One rule keeps this simple: **clicking never changes the selection**. The focused record is a view. The
selection, next, is the thing the Workbench records and can replay.

### 3. A selection you can read back

![Ski Hill Drive selected from the header box](assets/screenshots/workbench-03-select.png){ .screenshot }
*Ski Hill Drive: 20 links, status `resolved`, and the GMNS selection fragment that names them. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

Type `Ski Hill Drive` into the **Find** tab's box and press **Select**. The resolver matches the phrase against
the network's own street names, finds the facility, and marks its 20 links. The **Find** tab shows three
things worth reading:

- The **status**, `resolved`: the phrase mapped to one unambiguous set of links. Other statuses are
  `ambiguous` (next step) and the empty result when nothing matched.
- The **diagnostics**: how it got there (`facility ['Ski Hill Drive']: 20 link(s)`).
- The **fragment**: a JSON document in the GMNS selection schema, the portable form of the selection. As a
  **Link list** it holds only the `link_id`s; as a **Segment** it keeps the street name and the from/to nodes
  instead, so another tool, or a later version of this network, can resolve it again. Pick the form and the
  ID system (GMNS, OpenStreetMap or Overture GERS) under **Export**, or a ProjectCard facility instead, and use
  the copy button on the box.

Why it matters: a selection made by name is reproducible in a way a hand-drawn box is not. The strip at the
bottom already shows it as `app.do(Select(utterance='Ski Hill Drive'))`; after an edit, a query selection is
resolved again against the edited network. With `--provider stub` the phrase is parsed by an offline pattern
matcher; the same box can use a local model through Ollama or a hosted one, and the selection object looks the
same either way.

### 4. What an ambiguous anchor means

![An ambiguous selection: candidate nodes for the anchor, as rings on the map](assets/screenshots/workbench-04-ambiguous.png){ .screenshot }
*"Cherry Street between Prospect Street and West Center Street": the `to` anchor could be node 60 or node 61. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

Now select `Cherry Street between Prospect Street and West Center Street`. A "between" phrase has a facility
(Cherry Street) and two **anchors**, the cross streets that bound the stretch; each anchor must resolve to one
node on the facility. The `from` anchor does (`Prospect Street → node 53`). The `to` anchor doesn't: West
Center Street meets Cherry Street at more than one node, so the resolver picks the nearest (node 60) and
reports the status **ambiguous**, with node 61 listed as the other candidate and both drawn as rings on the
map.

That status is the point. The resolver could have quietly taken its best guess, and three links would have
lit up looking exactly like a confident answer. Instead the selection says it is a guess, the tab badge shows
`?`, and export is refused until you settle it. Settling it is a **pin**: click `node 61` to choose it, or
**Pin node 60** to keep the resolver's choice. The selection is resolved again, the status becomes `resolved`,
and the pin becomes part of the selection's query (`app.do(PinAnchor(role='to', node_id=60))`), so it survives
an edit and comes back when you reuse a saved selection. **Unpin** returns to the resolver's choice.

Real networks are full of this: a cross street that crosses twice, a divided road with two carriageways, a
name shared by a street and a ramp. A selection status you can read is what lets you trust the selections you
didn't check by hand.

### 5. What validation severities mean

![The Validate panel after Run validation](assets/screenshots/workbench-05-issues.png){ .screenshot }
*After Run validation: 271 warnings and 16 info, and a dot on the map for every issue with a place. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

**Run validation** (the play icon in the **Validate** tab) runs two kinds of check and lists them together,
each with a severity:

- **error** — the network breaks the spec in a way a consumer can't work around: a required table or field is
  missing, a value has the wrong type, a foreign key points at a row that doesn't exist. Leavenworth has none.
- **warning** — something is wrong or can't be shown to be right. The spec check finds none on Leavenworth.
  The quality rules add 271: `quality.high_speed_residential`, a residential link whose `free_speed` (40) is above
  the 35 mph threshold. The spec allows it; the rule says it is probably a coding mistake, and its `fix_hint`
  says what to do if the speed is right (raise the facility class instead).
- **info** — worth knowing, not wrong: 16 `structural.missing_optional_resource` findings, one per optional
  GMNS table (`movement`, `segment`, `signal_*`, `zone`, ...) that this network doesn't include.

The status line sums them: `Validated v0: 271 warnings, 16 info`, the `v0` being the version of the network
that was checked. Spec checks are about whether the file is valid GMNS; quality rules are about whether the
network is plausible, and they are configurable (**Settings → Validation**, keyed by rule code), so a region
with 40 mph residential streets can raise the threshold instead of silencing the rule.

Each located issue is a dot on the map, colored by severity; click one in the list (or its crosshair "zoom
to" icon) and the map flies to its link, Inspect shows the record, and the table scrolls to the row. Findings
about a whole table, like the missing-resource notes, have no place on the map; findings that share a code and
differ only by resource are grouped into one row under a collapsed **Unlocated findings** block. The filters
(severity, table, code) carry counts, so `quality.high_speed_residential (271)` is one click away from being
the only thing in the list.

### 6. What an edit does to the network

![Fixing a free_speed value from an issue; the Edit tab shows the pending edit](assets/screenshots/workbench-06-fix.png){ .screenshot }
*Fix on an issue: the editor opens on the issue's column; Apply sends one edit; the Edit tab records it at v1. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

Press **Fix** on a `quality.high_speed_residential` issue. The editor opens on that record and that column
(`link 1 · free_speed`), prefilled with `40`, and with the issue as the edit's note, which you can replace
with your own reason (`Residential street: posted 35 mph`). Change the value to `35` and press **Apply**.

Three things happen, and each is visible:

- **The network version moves.** The network you opened was `v0`; it is now `v1`. Edits change the network in
  memory only; nothing on disk is touched until you save a copy, and the source is never overwritten. The
  version is what the rest of the Workbench keys on: the map and table redraw for `v1`, the stored validation
  is marked stale (`the network changed since: re-run`), and a delete planned on `v0` would be refused.
- **The edit log grows.** The **Edit** tab lists `#1 link 1: free_speed = 35.0 (Residential street: posted
  35 mph)`, with the rows it touched (`1 link`) and the version it produced (`v1`), and says `1 unsaved`; the
  network picker says the same, and the header's validity light turns amber-outlined. The undo icon reverses
  the newest edit; undo is last-in, first-out and is itself recorded (`app.do(UndoEdit())`). A redo icon beside
  it would reapply that edit (`app.do(RedoEdit())`) until any other change clears it.
- **The edited rows are re-checked at once.** A value the spec disagrees with, such as a foreign key to a row
  that doesn't exist or a required field left empty, is applied anyway and listed under **Edit warnings** in
  the **Edit** tab with its own **Fix**, so you can put it right where you found it. A speed of 35 raises
  no warning, so the count stays at 0.

Why it matters: an edit in the Workbench is a typed action with a note, a version and an undo, not a cell
changed in a spreadsheet. That is what makes the next two steps possible.

### 7. What "Session as Python" is for

![Session as Python: the whole session as a replayable script](assets/screenshots/workbench-07-python.png){ .screenshot }
*Every action you took, as the script that repeats it. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

The strip at the bottom of the window shows the last action as Python; the code icon in the footer (tooltip
"Copy session as Python") shows the whole session as one script: the imports, `app = Session()`, and one
`app.do(...)` line per action, from `OpenNetwork(source=...)` through `Select`, `PinAnchor`, `RunValidation`,
`EditCells` and `UndoEdit`.

It exists because clicking is a bad way to document work. The script is the record of what you did to the
network, in the form a reviewer can read, a colleague can run on the next quarter's network, and a CI job can
run on every one. A build you approved replays with `approved=True`; a save replays as a new copy. The one
thing to know before replaying: a folder you trusted on the `netstead app` command line is not in the script,
so a fresh `Session()` needs it in `io.allowed_roots` (see
[Every action is replayable](cookbook/workbench.md#every-action-is-replayable)).

### 8. Saving a copy, and what stays the same

![Save a copy: the edited network written to a new folder](assets/screenshots/workbench-08-save.png){ .screenshot }
*Save a copy as a Parquet folder. The source folder is never written to. (screenshot predates the panel restructure)*

The **Save** icon in the header opens a dialog that writes the network as it is now (`v1`, with your fix) to
a **new** folder or file: name it, choose Parquet, CSV, DuckDB or Zip, and pick a folder inside your home
directory with **Choose folder…** and **Use this folder**, then **Save**. The save is a job; when it finishes
a toast says where the copy went and which tables differ from the source, the edit is marked `saved` in the
Edit tab, and the unsaved badge clears.

What stays the same is the network you opened. The Workbench never writes to its source, local or remote, and
never overwrites an existing copy, so an afternoon of edits can't damage the file you started from. Open
warnings are listed and confirmed before a save goes ahead. A Parquet copy opens directly in GeoLibre, QGIS or
ArcGIS Pro, and feeds AequilibraE, DTALite and Path4GMNS; see
[The Workbench and other tools](workbench-and-other-tools.md) for how to move between them.

# netstead cookbook

Each recipe is one task, one runnable example, one paragraph of why-it-works. Recipes are intentionally short — for the *design* behind a workflow, follow the "See also" link to the relevant concept page.

For generic Frictionless data-package recipes (S3 reads, format conversion, generic spatial scope), see the [corral cookbook](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/cookbook/).

## Validation + data quality

* [Run validation and read the report](validate-network.md) — interpret severity / category / code.
* [Customize the data-quality rule pack](customize-quality.md) — threshold overrides, disable rules, plug in your own.
* [Triage findings, propose fixes, apply them](fix-findings.md) — propose fixes on individual findings in the viewer, download them as a YAML edit log, replay it in Python.

## Creating networks

* [Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture](build-from-osm.md) — `netstead build --source osm` (needs the `[osm]` extra) or `--source overture` (needs `[overture]`) from a place / bbox / point+buffer.

## Scope + geographic subsetting

* [Build a scope from seed nodes](scope-from-nodes.md) — BFS shortest-path, network buffers, FK pushdown.

For bbox / polygon (non-GMNS-specific) spatial scope, see [corral cookbook: spatial scope](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/cookbook/scope-bbox/).

## Querying + editing linked tables

* [Query and update linked tables](query-and-update.md) — join across foreign keys, inspect lazily (no pandas), edit rows Network-Wrangler-style with rollback.
* [Edit a network with atomic rollback](edit-with-rollback.md) — `Session` lifecycle, dry-run preview, persisted history.

## Surfaces

* [View a network on a map](view-your-network.md) — render a self-contained Leaflet map of any GMNS network, with or without validation overlays.
* [Explore networks in the Netstead Workbench](workbench.md) — linked map + tables, validation with fixes, NL selection, replayable actions.
* [Find links by describing them](find-links.md) — what you can type ("Cedar St between Central Ave and Price Ave", "all residential links"), which requests need a language model, and how fast each is; in the Workbench, `netstead select` or Python.
* [Write a Workbench plugin](workbench-plugins.md) — add Actions, settings, state, routes and a front end as a separate pip package; the `Host` API, trust model, testing and versioning.
* [Author ProjectCards in the Workbench](workbench-project-cards.md) — the project cards plugin: select, change, preview and commit network_wrangler ProjectCards.
* [Run language models locally with Ollama](local-llm-ollama.md) — install Ollama, pull `qwen3:4b`, select in plain English with nothing leaving your machine.
* [Self-host the HTTP server](serve-http.md) — config file, bearer auth, deploying behind a proxy.
* [Wire the MCP server to Claude Code / Claude Desktop](serve-mcp.md) — stdio transport, tool list, agent prompts.
* [Run the bundled benchmarks](run-bench.md) — `netstead bench` (load / validate / connectivity timings) and `netstead bench-suite` (create / selection / viz-pack), what to expect on Leavenworth vs regional networks.

## For AI agents specifically

* [Drive both packages from a tool-call loop](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/ai/json-cli/) — every CLI command emits a parseable document with `--json`.
* [AI surface overview](https://e-lo.github.io/netstead/corral/ai/) — llms.txt + api-index.json + Skills + MCP.

## Contributing a new recipe

A recipe is `kind: howto` per the [Page Style Guide](https://github.com/e-lo/netstead/blob/main/packages/netstead/docs/_page-style-guide.md) (a contributor page in the repo, not on this site):

* `When to use this` — 1-2 sentences, the trigger.
* `Quick example` — ≤20 lines, copy-pasteable against the Leavenworth fixture, with **prose before the code**.
* `Step-by-step` — numbered, one short paragraph each.
* `Common variations` — collapsible accordions (`???`), one per variation.
* `Pitfalls` — explicit gotchas.
* `See also` — one link per related concept, no diffuse paths.

Open a PR with the new recipe + a link from this index. CI runs every column-0 ```python fence in the docs (`packages/netstead/tests/test_documented_python_contract.py`) and fails if it raises; indented accordion / tab blocks and blocks preceded by `<!-- doctest: skip -->` are not executed, and printed output is not compared.

# CLI reference

## Summary

`netstead` is the command-line front door to the library: inspect, validate, convert, build, scope,
clean and benchmark GMNS networks, and start the HTTP, MCP and Workbench servers. The command tree
below is generated from the live typer app (`netstead.cli.app`) on every docs build, so it cannot
drift from the installed version; `netstead --help` and `netstead <command> --help` print the same
text in the terminal.

Three conventions apply across the tree:

- **`--json`.** Every data command accepts `--json` and then writes exactly one JSON document to
  stdout, so the result pipes into `jq` or straight into an agent. The index table marks which
  commands take it.
- **`netstead doctor`** is an *install* doctor: Python version, optional extras, vendored spec
  versions, and whether the bundled Leavenworth fixture loads. To diagnose a network, use
  `netstead validate` (spec, schema and foreign-key checks) or `netstead quality` (data-quality rules).
- **Optional extras.** Commands that need an extra (`server`, `mcp`, `clean`, `osm`, `reports`, ...)
  are always listed in `--help`. When the extra is missing they exit with code 1 and one line on
  stderr, `netstead.<module> requires the [<extra>] extra: pip install 'netstead[<extra>]'`, which
  names the extra to install; `netstead doctor` shows which extras are present.

## Commands

{% raw %}
```text
Usage: netstead [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--install-completion` | flag |  | Install completion for the current shell. |
| `--show-completion` | flag |  | Show completion for the current shell, to copy it or customize the installation. |

| Command | What it does | `--json` |
|---|---|---|
| [`netstead validate`](#netstead-validate) | Validate ``source`` against the GMNS spec. | yes |
| [`netstead info`](#netstead-info) | Print GMNS-aware metadata about ``source`` — spec version + table summary. | yes |
| [`netstead convert`](#netstead-convert) | Convert a data package from any supported format to another. | yes |
| [`netstead quality`](#netstead-quality) | Run the GMNS data-quality rule pack against ``source``. | yes |
| [`netstead doctor`](#netstead-doctor) | Check your netstead install — Python version, extras, vendored specs. | yes |
| [`netstead bench`](#netstead-bench) | Run read/validate/connectivity benchmarks; print timings. | yes |
| [`netstead bench-suite`](#netstead-bench-suite) | Run the DuckDB-path benchmark suite (create / selection / viz-pack). |  |
| [`netstead build`](#netstead-build) | Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture and write it to ``DEST``. | yes |
| [`netstead select`](#netstead-select) | Resolve a natural-language selection to GMNS link/node ids. | yes |
| [`netstead select-serve`](#netstead-select-serve) | Serve the interactive selection map: now an alias of ``netstead app SOURCE``. |  |
| [`netstead viz`](#netstead-viz) | Serve the network viewer: now an alias of ``netstead app SOURCE``. |  |
| [`netstead app`](#netstead-app) | Serve the Netstead Workbench: open, inspect, and select on GMNS networks in the browser. |  |
| [`netstead spec`](#netstead-spec) | GMNS spec utilities — list and diff vendored versions. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead server`](#netstead-server) | Run the netstead self-hostable HTTP server. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead mcp`](#netstead-mcp) | Run the netstead MCP server for AI-agent access. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead clean`](#netstead-clean) | GMNS network-editing ops (requires the 'clean' extra). | per sub-command |
| [`netstead scope`](#netstead-scope) | Build a NetworkScope and print its (links, nodes) sets. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead index`](#netstead-index) | Spatial + graph index build/status/drop. | per sub-command |
| [`netstead llm`](#netstead-llm) | Language-model providers for natural-language features. | per sub-command |

### `netstead validate`

Validate ``source`` against the GMNS spec.

Runs the four-pass validator (structural / schema / foreign-key
/ sync-state) with the GMNS spec auto-loaded — so reading a
CSV directory without a ``datapackage.json`` gets the real
per-table schema checks, not the empty "every table is
unexpected" output of the generic ``corral validate``.

Exit code is non-zero iff any ERROR-severity issue is recorded.

Examples:
    Validate the bundled Leavenworth fixture as CSVs::

```text
        $ netstead validate path/to/leavenworth/csv

    Write the interactive map+table HTML viewer::

        $ netstead validate path/to/network --html report.html

    Export findings to a spreadsheet::

        $ netstead validate path/to/network --csv f.csv --xlsx f.xlsx
```

```text
Usage: netstead validate [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path / URL to a GMNS network (datapackage.json or CSV/Parquet/DuckDB directory). |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--spec` | text |  | Override the default GMNS spec version (e.g. '0.96'). Defaults to netstead.DEFAULT_SPEC. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout instead of rich panels. |
| `--all` | flag |  | List every finding on its own row instead of folding repeated structural findings into one. |
| `--html` | path |  | Write the interactive network-on-map HTML viewer to this path. Falls back to a table-only HTML report when the \[reports\] extra is not installed. |
| `--csv` | path |  | Write the flat findings table to this CSV path. |
| `--xlsx` | path |  | Write the flat findings table to this XLSX path (requires \[reports\] extra). |
| `--yes`, `-y` | flag |  | Auto-approve any gated ops (alternative to CORRAL_AUTO_APPROVE=1). |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead info`

Print GMNS-aware metadata about ``source`` — spec version + table summary.

```text
Usage: netstead info [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path / URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--spec` | text |  | Override the default GMNS spec version. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout instead of rich panels. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead convert`

Convert a data package from any supported format to another.

Loads ``source`` (any format corral can read) and writes the
same logical package to ``dest`` in the target format. Output
format is taken from ``--format`` when supplied, otherwise
inferred from the ``dest`` extension; an extension-less ``dest``
defaults to partitioned parquet (architecture §6.1).

```text
Usage: netstead convert [OPTIONS] SOURCE DEST
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Source data package path/URL. |
| `DEST` | path | yes | Destination path. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--format`, `-f` | text |  | Output format (csv/parquet/duckdb/zipcsv). Default: infer from dest extension; fall back to parquet. |
| `--engine` | text |  | Engine: DuckDB (the only compute engine). |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |
| `--yes`, `-y` | flag |  | Auto-approve gated ops. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead quality`

Run the GMNS data-quality rule pack against ``source``.

Each rule emits Severity.WARNING / INFO findings with category
DATA_QUALITY. The output is a ValidationReport (rendered as a
rich table or JSON document per ``--json``).

```text
Usage: netstead quality [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path / URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--spec` | text |  | Override the default GMNS spec version. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout instead of rich panels. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead doctor`

Check your netstead install — Python version, extras, vendored specs.

```text
This is an INSTALL doctor, not a network doctor. To diagnose a
specific GMNS network, use:

  netstead validate <path>    spec / schema / FK / sync-state checks
  netstead quality  <path>    data-quality rules (high speed on residential, etc.)
  netstead info     <path>    table list + row counts
```

Exits non-zero on any install failure.

```text
Usage: netstead doctor [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit checks as a JSON array. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead bench`

Run read/validate/connectivity benchmarks; print timings.

Phases timed (each via time.perf_counter):

* ``load`` — `Network.from_source`.
* ``validate`` — `Network.validate` (structural/schema only).
* ``links_count`` + ``nodes_count`` — trivial materialization sanity.
* ``is_connected`` — full graph index build + component count
  (skipped silently when the ``[graph]`` extra is missing).

Output is a dict with ``phases`` (list of ``{phase, seconds}``) and
a ``total_seconds`` summary. ``--json`` writes the dict to stdout for
machine consumption; otherwise rendered via the standard rich panel.

```text
Usage: netstead bench [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path/URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--engine` | text |  | Compute engine (DuckDB is the only one; kept for compatibility). |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead bench-suite`

Run the DuckDB-path benchmark suite (create / selection / viz-pack).

Sweeps the requested size tiers over the three operation families from
the benchmarking-suite scope, capturing wall-time and peak memory, and
emits one structured document. DuckDB (via ibis) is the single compute
engine; pandas / polars / pyarrow are I/O formats, so there is no engine
axis — the suite measures the DuckDB path and the binary store format.

``--format json`` (default) emits the canonical regression document;
``csv`` flattens the results; ``md`` renders the advertising table with
an environment stamp and the standing honesty caveats. Fixture
definitions live in ``benchmarks/fixtures.toml``; the L tier is resolved
from the ``NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE`` / ``NETSTEAD_BENCH_LARGE_BBOX`` env vars
(never committed).

```text
Usage: netstead bench-suite [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--sizes` | text | `S,M` | Size tiers to sweep (comma-separated: S,M,L). |
| `--operations` | text | `network_create,selection,viz_pack` | Operation families to run (comma-separated). |
| `--format` | text | `json` | Output format: json \| csv \| md. |
| `--output`, `-o` | path |  | Write to this file instead of stdout. |
| `--repeats` | integer | `3` | Macro timing repeats (reported as median + min). |
| `--warm-repeats` | integer | `20` | Repeats for the warm selection number. |
| `--run-osm` | flag |  | Include live OSM builds (hits Overpass). |
| `--fixtures` | path |  | Override path to a fixtures.toml. |
| `--commit` | text |  | Git SHA to stamp into the env block. |

### `netstead build`

Build a GMNS network from OpenStreetMap or Overture and write it to ``DEST``.

```text
Usage: netstead build [OPTIONS] DEST
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DEST` | path | yes | Output path for the GMNS network (dir or file). |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--place` | text |  | Place name to geocode (city/county/etc.). |
| `--bbox` | text |  | Bounding box 'west,south,east,north' (EPSG:4326). |
| `--point` | text |  | Center 'lat,lon'; use with --buffer. |
| `--buffer` | float | `0.0` | Buffer in metres around --point. |
| `--network-type` | text | `roads` | roads and/or paths; repeat the option or comma-separate (e.g. roads,paths). Deprecated: drive = roads; walk, bike, all = roads,paths. |
| `--extra-tags` | text |  | Comma-separated extra source properties/tags to carry. |
| `--source` | text | `osm` | Data source: 'osm' or 'overture'. |
| `--overture-release` | text |  | Overture release string (overture source only). |
| `--data-root` | text |  | Override Overture data base URI / local snapshot dir (overture source only). |
| `--engine` | text |  | Compute engine (DuckDB is the only one; kept for compatibility). |
| `--spec-version` | text |  | GMNS spec version (default: latest). |
| `--format` | text |  | Output format: csv / parquet / duckdb / zip. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit a JSON summary on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead select`

Resolve a natural-language selection to GMNS link/node ids.

Prints the validated selection fragment on success (exit 0). On an
ambiguous result it prints the status, the provisional link ids, each
anchor with the other nodes it could be, and diagnostics (exit 3); on
not-found it prints diagnostics (exit 1).

With a language model chosen and ``select.grammar_first`` on (the default),
the offline grammar is tried first and the model is called only when it
can't read the request with names the network has, as in the Workbench.

```text
Usage: netstead select [OPTIONS] UTTERANCE SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `UTTERANCE` | text | yes | e.g. "I-40 EB between Harrison Ave and NC 54". |
| `SOURCE` | text | yes | Path/URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--provider` | text |  | Parser: stub \| anthropic \| openai \| gemini \| ollama (default: settings). |
| `--model` | text |  | Model id (default: settings, else the provider default; see `netstead llm status`). |
| `--engine` | text |  | Compute engine (DuckDB is the only one; kept for compatibility). |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead select-serve`

Serve the interactive selection map: now an alias of ``netstead app SOURCE``.

```text
Usage: netstead select-serve [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | text | yes | Path/URL to a GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--provider` | text |  | NL parser: stub \| anthropic \| openai \| gemini \| ollama (default: settings). |
| `--engine` | text |  | Ignored: DuckDB is the only engine (kept for compatibility). |
| `--host` | text |  | Bind host. |
| `--port` | integer |  | Bind port. |

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |

### `netstead app`

Serve the Netstead Workbench: open, inspect, and select on GMNS networks in the browser.

```text
Usage: netstead app [OPTIONS] [SOURCES]...
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCES` | text | no | GMNS network paths/URLs to open. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--provider` | text |  | NL parser: stub \| anthropic \| openai \| gemini \| ollama (default: settings). |
| `--model` | text |  | NL model id (default: settings, else the provider default; see `netstead llm status`). |
| `--basemap` | text |  | Basemap: positron \| esri (default: settings). |
| `--host` | text |  | Bind host (default: settings, 127.0.0.1). |
| `--port` | integer |  | Bind port (default: settings, 8850). |

### `netstead spec`

GMNS spec utilities — list and diff vendored versions.

```text
Usage: netstead spec [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Sub-commands**

- [`netstead spec list`](#netstead-spec-list) — List the GMNS spec versions vendored in this build of netstead.
- [`netstead spec diff`](#netstead-spec-diff) — Diff two vendored GMNS spec versions resource-by-resource.

#### `netstead spec list`

List the GMNS spec versions vendored in this build of netstead.

```text
Usage: netstead spec list [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON instead of a rich table. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

#### `netstead spec diff`

Diff two vendored GMNS spec versions resource-by-resource.

```text
Usage: netstead spec diff [OPTIONS] V1 V2
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `V1` | text | yes | Baseline GMNS spec version (e.g. 0.96). |
| `V2` | text | yes | Comparison GMNS spec version (e.g. 0.97). |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON instead of a rich summary. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead server`

Run the netstead self-hostable HTTP server.

```text
Usage: netstead server [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Sub-commands**

- [`netstead server run`](#netstead-server-run) — Start the netstead HTTP server with config from ``--config``.

#### `netstead server run`

Start the netstead HTTP server with config from ``--config``.

Reads `corral.api.ServerSettings` from the config
file (or uses defaults — localhost, no packages, auth=bearer
with no token, which fails fast on first request).

The CLI ``--bind`` / ``--port`` flags override the matching
config keys for one-off testing without editing the file.

```text
Usage: netstead server run [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--config`, `-c` | path |  | Path to server config (YAML/JSON). |
| `--bind` | text |  | Override config bind address (default 127.0.0.1). |
| `--port` | integer |  | Override config port (default 8000). |

### `netstead mcp`

Run the netstead MCP server for AI-agent access.

```text
Usage: netstead mcp [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Sub-commands**

- [`netstead mcp serve`](#netstead-mcp-serve) — Start the netstead MCP server on stdio (for Claude Desktop / Claude Code).

#### `netstead mcp serve`

Start the netstead MCP server on stdio (for Claude Desktop / Claude Code).

Configure your MCP client to launch ``netstead mcp serve`` as a
subprocess (typical example:

.. code-block:: json

```text
    {"mcpServers": {"netstead": {"command": "netstead", "args": ["mcp", "serve"]}}}
```

). Tools exposed: ``describe_network``, ``validate_package``,
``quality_check``, ``connected_components``, ``scope_from_nodes``,
plus the generic corral tools.

```text
Usage: netstead mcp serve [OPTIONS]
```

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--name` | text | `netstead` | MCP server display name. |

### `netstead clean`

GMNS network-editing ops (requires the 'clean' extra).

```text
Usage: netstead clean [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Sub-commands**

- [`netstead clean simplify-geometry`](#netstead-clean-simplify-geometry) — Simplify link geometries on the network at ``source``.
- [`netstead clean merge-close-nodes`](#netstead-clean-merge-close-nodes) — Merge node pairs within ``--threshold-m`` of each other; rewrite incident links.
- [`netstead clean remove-orphans`](#netstead-clean-remove-orphans) — Drop nodes with no incident links.
- [`netstead clean recompute-lengths`](#netstead-clean-recompute-lengths) — Recompute ``link.length`` from the inline geometry column.

#### `netstead clean simplify-geometry`

Simplify link geometries on the network at ``source``.

```text
Usage: netstead clean simplify-geometry [OPTIONS] SOURCE
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path to the GMNS network to edit. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--dest` | path |  | Where to write the modified network. Default: overwrite source. |
| `--mode` | text | `redundant_only` | redundant_only or douglas_peucker. |
| `--tolerance` | float | `0.0` | Tolerance in CRS units (douglas_peucker only). |
| `--engine` | text |  | Compute engine (DuckDB is the only one; kept for compatibility). |
| `--dry-run` | flag |  | Print what would change; do not write. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

#### `netstead clean merge-close-nodes`

| `--dry-run` | flag |  | Print what would change; do not write. |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

### `netstead scope`

Build a NetworkScope and print its (links, nodes) sets.

```text
Usage: netstead scope [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...
```

**Sub-commands**

- [`netstead scope from-nodes`](#netstead-scope-from-nodes) — Build a scope from seed node ids and print its (links, nodes) sets.
- [`netstead scope from-node`](#netstead-scope-from-node) — Scope = all nodes within ``--network-buffer`` network-distance of ``node_id``.
- [`netstead scope connected-component`](#netstead-scope-connected-component) — Scope = the weakly-connected component containing ``seed_node_id``.
- [`netstead scope from-zone`](#netstead-scope-from-zone) — Scope = all nodes with ``zone_id`` in ``zone_ids`` plus their incident links.

#### `netstead scope from-nodes`

Build a scope from seed node ids and print its (links, nodes) sets.

```text
Usage: netstead scope from-nodes [OPTIONS] SOURCE NODE_IDS...
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path to the GMNS network. |
| `NODE_IDS` | integer | yes | Seed node ids. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--path-between`, `--no-path-between` | flag | on |  |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

#### `netstead scope from-node`

Scope = all nodes within ``--network-buffer`` network-distance of ``node_id``.

```text
Usage: netstead scope from-node [OPTIONS] SOURCE NODE_ID
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path to the GMNS network. |
| `NODE_ID` | integer | yes | Seed node id. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--network-buffer` | text | `0.5mi` | Distance with unit (e.g. '0.5mi', '800m'). |
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

#### `netstead scope connected-component`

Scope = the weakly-connected component containing ``seed_node_id``.

```text
Usage: netstead scope connected-component [OPTIONS] SOURCE SEED_NODE_ID
```

**Arguments**

| Argument | Type | Required | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `SOURCE` | path | yes | Path to the GMNS network. |

**Options**

| Option | Type | Default | Help |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--json` | flag |  | Emit JSON on stdout. |

Machine-readable: `--json` writes the result to stdout as JSON.

#### `netstead scope from-zone`

### `netstead llm`

Language-model providers for natural-language features.


**Sub-commands**

- [`netstead llm remove-key`](#netstead-llm-remove-key) — Delete PROVIDER's key from the OS keyring. Env vars are yours to unset.
- [`netstead llm test`](#netstead-llm-test) — Make an authenticated call that spends no tokens (list models); exit 1 on failure.
- [`netstead llm models`](#netstead-llm-models) — List the models offered for PROVIDER: the catalog, or the installed models for Ollama.
- [`netstead llm pull`](#netstead-llm-pull) — Download MODEL into the configured Ollama server (llm.ollama.base_url), with progress.

## Examples

Check the install, then summarize and validate a network. `--json` turns the summary into one
JSON document; `--html` writes the interactive validation report next to the terminal output.

```bash
netstead doctor
netstead info ./my-network --json
netstead validate ./my-network --html report.html
```

---
title: Workbench HTTP API reference
audience: both
kind: reference
summary: Every route the Workbench server exposes, grouped by area, generated from its OpenAPI document at build time.
---

# Workbench HTTP API reference

## Summary

`netstead app` serves one Workbench `Session` as a local web app. The browser front end is only a
client of the routes below; anything it does, a script can do with `curl` or an HTTP library. The
route list is generated on every docs build from the FastAPI app's OpenAPI document
(`build_app(session).openapi()`), so it cannot drift from the code; a running server serves the same
document at `/openapi.json` and interactive docs at `/docs`.

Every state change goes through one route, `POST /api/actions`, whose body is one Action (a JSON
object discriminated on its `type`). The Action schemas are on the
[Workbench Actions](workbench-actions.md) page; `GET /api/actions` returns the JSON schema of every
Action the running session accepts, plugin Actions included. Reads are plain `GET`s and never
recorded in the history.

### Events (`GET /api/events`)

The stream is Server-Sent Events (`text/event-stream`). It opens with a `state` event carrying the
full session snapshot (the same payload as `GET /api/state`) and then carries every event the
session publishes, each frame named by its `type`:

- `state` — a fresh snapshot after any change (open, close, selection, settings, edits).
- `history` — one recorded Action, in the shape `GET /api/history` lists.
- `job` — a background job's snapshot at each stage change (open, build, validate, save and Ollama
  pulls run as jobs; `POST /api/actions` answers `202` with the job and the outcome arrives here).
- `llm` — provider and key status after a key is set or removed or a model pulled.
- `navigate` — a map navigation request raised by a `Navigate` Action.

A `: keepalive` comment is sent after 15 seconds of silence so proxies keep the connection open;
`?max_events=N` closes the stream after `N` events, for scripts and tests.

### Local-bind guards

On the default loopback bind the server answers `400` to any request whose `Host` header is not
`localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`, and `403` to any state-changing request that names a foreign
`Origin` or arrives `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`; see
[Explore in the Workbench](../cookbook/workbench.md#quick-start) for what that means when you
expose the app.

### Plugin routes

Each installed plugin's router is mounted under `/api/plugins/<id>/` and its static files under
`/plugins/<id>/`. Those routes depend on what is installed, so they are not listed here;
`GET /api/plugins` names the installed plugins and their state.

## Routes

{% raw %}
### Session

The session as a whole: its state, settings, history and the Action bus.

#### `GET /api/state`

Responses: `200` Successful Response

#### `GET /api/config`

Responses: `200` Successful Response

#### `GET /api/settings`

Responses: `200` Successful Response

#### `GET /api/history`

Every entry, plus the import lines that head them as a script ("copy session as Python").

A nested entry (``parent_seq`` set) is written as a comment, since replaying its parent repeats
it, so it needs no import.

Responses: `200` Successful Response

#### `GET /api/actions`

Every Action this session accepts, with its owner and JSON schema. Read-only; nothing is recorded.

Responses: `200` Successful Response

#### `POST /api/actions`

Apply an action. A job action (open/build) answers 202 with its job; the outcome arrives over SSE.

Request body: a JSON object (free-form; see the description).

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/events`

SSE stream: a ``state`` snapshot first, then every published event.

``max_events`` closes the stream after that many events (tests and scripted clients).

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_events` | query | integer or null | no |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

### Jobs

Background jobs started by job Actions (open, build, validate, save) and by Ollama pulls.

#### `GET /api/jobs`

Every background job this session started, newest first.

Responses: `200` Successful Response

#### `POST /api/jobs/{job_id}/cancel`

Request cancellation; it takes effect at the job's next stage boundary.

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `job_id` | path | string | yes |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

### Files, URLs and build estimates

What the **Open / Import** dialog calls: folders inside `io.allowed_roots`, remote GMNS URLs, place search, and sizing a `build_network` request before approving it.

#### `GET /api/fs/list`

List a folder inside ``io.allowed_roots`` (no ``path``: the roots themselves).

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | query | string or null | no |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `POST /api/check-url`

Reachability, credential *source* name, and tables for a remote GMNS URL.

Request body: a JSON object (free-form; see the description).

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/geocode`

Nominatim place candidates (bbox + simplified outline) for the Area step.

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `q` | query | string | yes |  |
| `limit` | query | integer | no | `8` |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `POST /api/estimate`

Size a ``build_network`` request (pre-query + model) without running it.

Request body: a JSON object (free-form; see the description).

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

### Network data

Per open network. `{net_id}` is the id `GET /api/state` lists for the network; `{component}` is the component within it (`roadway` for the GMNS tables).

#### `GET /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/network.bin`

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `net_id` | path | string | yes |  |
| `component` | path | string | yes |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/network.attrs.json`

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `net_id` | path | string | yes |  |
| `component` | path | string | yes |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/properties`

The columns that can color (or size) the ``link`` table's features, or the ``node`` table's.

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/issues/summary`

The issues that match every filter, folded by code and severity (largest severity, then count, first).

The Validate list groups from this, never from a page of ``/issues``; a group's members are then paged with
``/issues?code=…&severity=…``. ``facets`` are over the whole set, as in ``/issues``.

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `net_id` | path | string | yes |  |
| `component` | path | string | yes |  |
| `severity` | query | string or null | no |  |
| `table` | query | string or null | no |  |
| `code` | query | string or null | no |  |
| `located` | query | `yes` / `no` or null | no |  |
| `record` | query | string or null | no |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/issues/anchors`

Where one finding type sits on the map: its link ids, node ids and bare coordinates (all of them).

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `net_id` | path | string | yes |  |
| `component` | path | string | yes |  |
| `code` | query | string | yes |  |
| `severity` | query | string or null | no |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

### Validation and edits

The last validation run's issues and report, and the pending-edit ledger.

| `code` | query | string or null | no |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/issues/markers`

| `component` | path | string | yes |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/report.html`

The offline validation report (the ``render_validation_html`` page) for the last, still-current run.

The page is drawn from the network the run read (``IssueSet.network``); the version check only refuses a
report the network has moved on from.

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `net_id` | path | string | yes |  |
| `component` | path | string | yes |  |

Responses: `200` Successful Response · `422` Validation Error

#### `GET /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/edits`

Pending edits, undo and dirty state, and the live edit warnings (always current, never stale).

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |

| `component` | path | string | yes |  |

#### `POST /api/n/{net_id}/{component}/table/{table_name}/delete-plan`

A dry run of ``DeleteRows``: rows per table that would go, or why the deletion is refused.

| Parameter | In | Type | Required | Default |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `net_id` | path | string | yes |  |
